The original paper reported a beta coefficient for cognitive ability (controlling for prior grades) of .09 and a t = 3.22, significant at alpha = .01. In our reproduction we found beta = .08, t = 3.11. The delta R^2 was similar, although not sufficiently close, .02 in original research vs. .01 in our reproduction. During the back-and-forth discussion regarding which outcomes to include as criteria, we inadvertently did not replace one such outcome in the Analyst success criteria section. repro_pattern_description: Reproduction result: The focal test of reproducibility, per the preregistration, uses the pre-computed ratios of Actual to Perceived Arm length that the authors provided. The sample size available for these columns in the data matched the original report, with 15 left-handed and 15 right-handed participants. Reproducing the focal test ANOVA gives a result of F(1, 28) = 4.74, p=0.038. The p value of 0.038 translates to p_rep = 0.8952, which rounds to p_rep = .90. Thus, the inferential statistics are reproducible in terms of sample size, F value and p value. The effect size reported by the authors (partial eta squared) is not precisely reproducible but is consistent with a very minor rounding error. The sum of squares (SS) for the effect is 0.01542, and the SS for the error is 0.09108. Since partial eta squared = SSE_effect / (SS_effect + SS_error), this gives 0.1447, which does not round to 0.15. However, this is a minor difference: If the output of the statistical software used by the researchers rounded this to 0.145, they could then have reasonably and accurately rounded this to 0.15. The secondary aspect of reproducibility we preregistered was asking whether the precomputed ratios of actual to perceived arm length, computed by the authors in the data file and used for the above analysis, match what you get from recomputing these ratios using the raw data provided for actual and perceived arm length separately. For 100% of the left arm ratios (Perceived Left Arm Length / Actual Left Arm Length) these match precisely. They match precisely for only 29 out of the 30 right arm ratios, however: the other participant has a precomputed ratio of 1.111779 but when recomputed from the raw values, this ratio is 1.114458 (a very minor difference of 0.00267). Using the re-computed ratios gives an ANOVA result of F(1, 28) = 4.71, p=0.0386, p_rep=0.894, partial eta squared=0.1439, a very minor difference from the reported result.

repro_pattern_criteria: Reproduction Criteria: A successful reproduction of the key SCORE claim would involve that two elements are observed graphically: - Native-born white women in 1980 had lower college completion rate than men. Graphically, the “left square is above the right circle.” - Native-born white women in 2005 had completed college at approximately the same rate as their male counterpart. Graphically, the “right square broadly overlaps with the right circle.”  The focal hypothesis as formulated by SCORE does not require more stringent criteria. Indeed, the graphical nature of the claim makes it difficult to “see” what the exact levels are (especially because the scales are imprecise, and the graphical symbols are large).  One can make an educated guess from the figure however about the following more stringent three criteria: - Native-born white women in 1980 had about 20% college completion rates. - Native-born white men in 1980 had about 25-30% college completion rates. - Native-born white women and men in 2005 had about 30-35% college completion rates.  Note that the original study does not report the regression estimates on which this portion of Figure 2 is based. Therefore, it is impossible to provide statistics related to the precision of these estimates, such as p-values, for a comparison with the original study.
repro_pattern_description: Reproduction Result: The reproduction is based on the computation of expected values from mean characteristics based on estimates from a logistic regression on two subsamples: the male subsample (35,954 observations) and the female subsample (37,751 observations). As explained in section 13 of the preregistration document (https://osf.io/aexnc/), the original study does not provide sample sizes. The reproduction attempt therefore cannot compare sample sizes. However, based on comparison with other sample sizes reported in the original study, one can infer that sample sizes in the original study and the reproduction are similar—again, see section 13 of the preregistration document.  Results are reported in Figure 1 below (also available as a png file at https://osf.io/ek3jr/). One can observe the following two elements: - Native-born white women in 1980 had lower college completion rate than men. Graphically, the “left square is above the right circle.” - Native-born white women in 2005 had completed college at almost approximately the same rate as their male counterpart. Graphically, the “right square is slightly below the right circle.”  More precisely, from the analysis data used to generate this figure: - Native-born white women in 1980 had 14.6% college completion rates. - Native-born white men in 1980 had 27.3% college completion rates. - Native-born white women in 2005 had 36.1% college completion rates. - Native-born white men in 2005 had 32.5% college completion rates.  Overall, the replication of the claim was almost successful according to the SCORE criteria: - It is successful in the comparison of men and women college completion rates in 1980 (men > women). - It is moderately successful in the comparison of men and women completion rates in 2008 (women ~> men). - It is successful on levels of men college completion rates in 1980 (27.3∈ [25-30]). - It is unsuccessful on levels of women college completion rates in 1980 (14.6 < 20). - It is successful on levels of men college completion rates in 2008 (32.5∈ [30-35]). - It is close to successful on levels of women college completion rates in 2008 (36.1 > 35).  It is worth highlighting however that in broader terms, the original claim that “women experienced substantially more intergenerational mobility than their male counterparts” is entirely verified in this reproduction.
